title: Quantum Computing
tagline: From thought experiments to error-corrected processors.

events.title: Feynman proposes quantum simulation
events.text: Richard Feynman argues that classical computers cannot efficiently simulate quantum physics, suggesting computers built on quantum mechanics instead.

events.title: Deutsch formalises the quantum computer
events.text: David Deutsch describes a universal quantum computer and the quantum Turing machine, outlining the theoretical machine that enables quantum algorithms.

events.title: Shor’s factoring algorithm
events.text: Peter Shor shows a quantum computer could factor large integers in polynomial time, threatening RSA-style cryptography and energising the field.

events.title: Grover’s search algorithm
events.text: Lov Grover invents a quantum search algorithm providing a quadratic speedup over any classical search — one of the few speedups that endure.

events.title: First working 2-qubit processor
events.text: A group led by Isaac Chuang runs a two-qubit NMR quantum search, one of the first experimental quantum information processors.

references.label: Nuclear magnetic resonance quantum computer — Wikipedia

events.title: IBM factors 15 with 7 qubits
events.text: IBM researchers run Shor’s algorithm on a 7-qubit NMR processor, factoring 15 into 3×5 — the first full execution of a quantum algorithm that a classical computer cannot outperform at scale.

events.title: D-Wave One: first commercial quantum computer
events.text: D-Wave Systems sells the D-Wave One to Lockheed Martin, marketing the first commercially available quantum annealing system.

events.title: Quantum supremacy with Sycamore
events.text: Google reports that its 53-qubit Sycamore chip performed a sampling task in ~200 seconds a classical supercomputer could not, claiming “quantum supremacy”.

events.title: IBM Eagle: 127 qubits
events.text: IBM unveils Eagle, a 127-qubit superconducting processor, the first IBM processor with more than 100 qubits.

events.title: The logical qubit era begins
events.text: University of Wisconsin–Madison and Google groups demonstrate logical qubits with error rates that fall as the code distance grows — the key step toward fault-tolerant machines.
